traveler: Anton Fugger, Reichsgraf, Regierer of the Fugger company
title: The Third Nephew: Anton Fugger, the Emperor's Purse, and the Turn from Money to Land
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Augsburg, Fuggerhäuser: the third son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Neue Deutsche Biographie gives 10 June 1493 at Augsburg. The exact house of birth is not documented; the pin is the family's Augsburg seat on the Maximilianstrasse, inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the tenth of June a third son is born to Georg Fugger and Regina Imhof in the family houses on the Maximilianstrasse. The Fugger von der Lilie are already the richest merchant house in the Empire, and his uncle Jakob is building a bank on Tyrolean silver and Hungarian copper. Anton is the youngest of Georg's three sons. His brother Raymund is older, his cousin Hieronymus is older, and command of the firm is not expected to reach this one. Which house on the street he is born in is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerhäuser on the Maximilianstrasse, Augsburg, the family seat and counting house

stops.name: Augsburg, Fuggerhäuser: the guardian and the contract
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of Georg Fugger's death (1506) and for the 1512 partnership agreement among the nephews, both from the Neue Deutsche Biographie; the month and day of neither is given, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Georg Fugger dies and the boy of thirteen passes into the guardianship of his uncle Jakob, who is guardian and employer in the same breath. Six years later the nephews sign the partnership agreement that fixes how the house is held: shares, votes, and the rule that no partner draws his capital out alone. Anton is nineteen when he signs it. He learns the firm the way a clerk learns it, from inside the ledger, under a man who delegates nothing and trusts less. Jakob has no sons, and the contract of 1512 names no successor.
suggested_refs: The 1512 Fugger partnership agreement (Gesellschaftsvertrag) among Jakob's nephews

stops.name: Nuremberg, the first counting house
stops.date_confidence: attested that Nuremberg was one of the branches of Anton's rotating apprenticeship (Neue Deutsche Biographie, which names Nuremberg, Breslau, Buda, Italy and Tyrol); the specific year within c. 1512-1523 is not documented and 1513 is an ordering device. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: He is sent out on the rotation Jakob designed for the nephews, and Nuremberg comes first: the metal market of southern Germany, where Fugger copper is weighed against Nuremberg brass and the correspondence with Antwerp and Venice crosses a desk every morning. The training is not schooling, it is posting, and the branches are the school. His brother and his cousin are on the same rotation, and nobody in this counting house is told that the three of them are being compared. He keeps books, checks weights, and writes in the house hand.
suggested_refs: The Fugger factory at Nuremberg, station of Anton's apprenticeship

stops.name: Breslau, the branch on the Rynek
stops.date_confidence: attested as a posting (Neue Deutsche Biographie names Breslau among the branches of the apprenticeship); the year is undocumented and set to order the segment. No Fugger building in Breslau is located in the reachable sources, so the pin is the market square as city landmark.
stops.campa: The rotation carries him east to Breslau, where the Fugger factor sits astride the road between Silesian linen, Polish grain, and the copper coming up out of the Hungarian mountains. Here the house is a freight business as much as a bank: wagons, tolls, river stages, the price of a hundredweight in a market three weeks' travel away. He learns what the ledger in Augsburg cannot show, which is how long a thing takes to arrive and what it costs to wait for it. He is twenty-two and has not yet spent a full year in any one city.
suggested_refs: The Fugger factory at Breslau on the Silesian trade road

stops.name: Buda, the copper of the Thurzo partnership
stops.date_confidence: attested as a posting (Neue Deutsche Biographie); the year is an ordering device. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: At Buda he works inside the greatest single enterprise the family owns, the Upper Hungarian copper partnership with the Thurzo, whose ore travels from Neusohl to Danzig to Antwerp and comes back as money. The Thurzo know the mountains and the Fugger hold the money, and the whole concern rests on a royal licence. That is its only security: the goodwill of a Hungarian crown, revocable, worth nothing in a bad year. Nine years from now, as head of the house, he will come back to Hungary and buy that licence again.
suggested_refs: The Fugger-Thurzo Upper Hungarian copper company and its Neusohl works

stops.name: Rome, the Banchi and the introduction of Johann Eck
stops.date_confidence: attested that Anton spent several years in Rome and that he helped introduce the theologian Johann Eck at the papal court (Neue Deutsche Biographie); the residency is dated only c. 1518-1523 and the specific year of the Eck introduction is not given. The Fugger premises in Rome are not located in the reachable sources; pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: He spends several years in Rome, in the banking quarter by the Banchi where the curia's money is made and unmade, and he learns Italian, Latin, and the papal court. Here he helps present at that court the Ingolstadt theologian Johann Eck, who has come to procure a bull against a friar in Saxony. The bull is Exsurge Domine. The friar is Martin Luther, whose first grievance was the indulgence traffic whose proceeds the Fugger house transferred, counted, and took its share of. Anton is twenty-seven. Nothing in the record says he remarked on any of it.
suggested_refs: The bull Exsurge Domine (1520), procured at Rome by Johann Eck
martin_luther.journey.json, for the Augsburg interrogation of 1518 held in the Fugger house

stops.name: Schwaz, the power of attorney in the mountain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the detail: the Neue Deutsche Biographie has Jakob sending Anton and his cousin Ulrich with the factor Georg Hörmann to Tyrol in 1523 under a sovereign delivery contract; the dossier adds smelting at Rattenberg, which the reachable Rattenberg sources do not mention, so Rattenberg is not given a pin of its own and the posting is set at Schwaz. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: Jakob sends him into Tyrol with his cousin Ulrich and the factor Georg Hörmann, and with something he has given no nephew before: legal power to bind the company. Schwaz is the mountain the house was built on, silver hauled out under lease from a sovereign who is permanently in debt to the lessee. Hörmann is the factor and knows the ground; Ulrich is the cousin; the power to bind the company is in Anton's name as well. It is the first time he is not being taught but used. He signs for copper and for silver, in his own hand, on his uncle's account.
suggested_refs: The Fugger silver-mining complex at Schwaz in Tyrol, held under sovereign lease

stops.name: Schwaz, Hans Maler sets him down in oil
stops.date_confidence: attested for the existence and 1525 date of a Hans Maler portrait of Anton Fugger, now at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe (Neue Deutsche Biographie); a second Maler portrait is at the Louvre, inv. RF 2002 28, acquired 2002 and shown in Room 809. The sitting itself is not documented as to place or date within the year, and Schwaz is chosen because Hans Maler worked there.
stops.campa: The painter of Schwaz sets him down on limewood: a young man of thirty-two, dark cap, fur collar, a face that gives away nothing at all. He is painted as a merchant and not as a lord, because he is not yet a lord. Four centuries later one of these panels hangs in the Louvre and another at Karlsruhe, and a silverpoint by Hans Burgkmair sits in a Berlin print room. There is also a drawing at Veste Coburg given to Dürer, an attribution the Neue Deutsche Biographie itself signals as uncertain.
suggested_refs: Hans Maler, portrait of Anton Fugger, Musée du Louvre inv. RF 2002 28, Room 809, Richelieu
Hans Maler, portrait of Anton Fugger, 1525, Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe
Hans Burgkmair the Elder, silverpoint drawing, Kupferstichkabinett Berlin
sources: Musée du Louvre collections database, ark:/53355/cl010067346

stops.name: Augsburg, Fuggerhäuser: the testament of the twenty-second of December
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance by the Neue Deutsche Biographie, which has Jakob revising his testamentary arrangements to give Anton decisive managerial responsibility while Raymund and Hieronymus remain partners without command; the precise date of 22 December 1525 comes from the dossier and was not independently re-verified in this pass.
stops.campa: Eight days before he dies, Jakob Fugger the Rich writes down which nephew rules. It is not the eldest. Raymund and Hieronymus keep their shares, their votes, and their names on the house, and lose the command; Anton, thirty-two years old, gets the command and the responsibility that goes with it. Jakob had watched all three of them for fifteen years, across five branches, and had eight days left. Why the choice fell on the youngest is stated nowhere in the reachable record.
suggested_refs: Jakob Fugger's final testamentary disposition, Augsburg, December 1525

stops.name: Augsburg, Fuggerhäuser: the uncle dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Neue Deutsche Biographie gives 30 December 1525 for Jakob's death and Anton's succession at the age of thirty-two.
stops.campa: Jakob Fugger dies in his own house on the thirtieth of December and Anton is Regierer of the company before the year turns. English Wikipedia puts the assets he inherits at 2,032,652 gulden, a figure that mixes company and estate accounting and should not be read as one man's cash. What he actually inherits is a bank whose largest debtor is the Holy Roman Emperor and whose largest asset is a mining lease from that emperor's brother. In the pamphlet literature of Germany the family name has by now become a word for usury.
suggested_refs: The Fugger company inventory drawn up after Jakob's death

stops.name: Buda, the Hungarian company put back on its feet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the substance (Neue Deutsche Biographie: Anton negotiates a reconciliation restoring the legal position of the Fugger-Thurzo Upper Hungarian copper enterprise with the Hungarian crown); no month is given. The 1527 inventory recording company capital at about 1.6 million gulden is from the same source.
stops.campa: His first act as head of the house is repair work in Hungary, where the copper partnership's standing with the crown had been broken and has to be bought back. He gets it back, in the year the Hungarian army is destroyed at Mohács and the kingdom he has just finished negotiating with begins to come apart under the Ottomans. The following year an inventory ordered after Jakob's death sets the company's capital at about 1.6 million gulden. He has been in charge for eighteen months.
suggested_refs: The 1527 Fugger company inventory, ordered after Jakob Fugger's death

stops.name: Rome, the factoría closed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the closure of the Roman branch after the Sack of Rome (Neue Deutsche Biographie gives 1527); the month is not documented and June is set to follow the sack of May 1527. The dossier's fuller account of the closure was flagged by the verification pass as not independently re-confirmed.
stops.campa: In May the Emperor's unpaid army takes Rome and holds it for months. The Fugger house has kept a factoría there since before Anton was born, because the curia was a customer and the curia's money moved through banks. Now the Emperor's own soldiers have sacked the customer, and a house known to be the Emperor's creditor cannot go on trading in the ruins of the papal court. Anton closes the branch. He had lived in that quarter himself, learning its Latin and its arithmetic, less than a decade before.
suggested_refs: The Sack of Rome, May 1527, and the withdrawal of German banking houses from the curia

stops.name: Augsburg, the marriage contract with Anna Rehlinger
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage in 1527 to Anna Rehlinger von Horgau, daughter of Hans Rehlinger (Neue Deutsche Biographie, English and German Wikipedia); the contract date of 5 February 1527 is from the dossier, which also records that sources differ between late February and early March for the wedding itself. That divergence is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He marries Anna Rehlinger von Horgau, daughter of an Augsburg patrician house, and by the contract of the fifth of February the weavers' grandsons are married into the city's old families. The Fuggers had bought counties and been made nobles under Maximilian, but a patriciate is not something an emperor can grant; it has to be married into, inside the city, house by house. Anna is twenty-two. She will bear him children for twenty-one years and die of it.
suggested_refs: The Fugger-Rehlinger marriage contract, Augsburg, 5 February 1527

stops.name: Vienna, the siege paid for
stops.date_confidence: attested that Fugger credits and arms deliveries assisted the Habsburg defence during the 1529 Ottoman siege of Vienna (Neue Deutsche Biographie); the date given is the opening of the siege. There is no evidence that Anton was personally at Vienna, and none is claimed: the pin marks where his money went. Pin inherited byte-identical from joseph_oppenheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: Suleiman brings an army to the walls of Vienna in September and Ferdinand of Austria has no money to meet it. The credits and the arms deliveries that hold the city come, in part, out of Augsburg. Anton is not on the walls and never sees them; what he sends is paper, and what the paper buys is powder, pike, and the wages of men who will stand. The house is lending against a revenue that does not yet exist, to a prince whose brother already owes it more than he can pay. The siege lifts in October.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman siege of Vienna, September-October 1529, financed on the Habsburg side partly through Fugger credit

stops.name: Augsburg, the Diet of 1530 and the imperial count
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, not resolved. The Neue Deutsche Biographie dates Anton's elevation to Reichsgraf to 1526; German Wikipedia states 1530 twice and independently, in its Anton Fugger and its Babenhausen articles. A third and separate act is documented for 20 June 1535, when Ferdinand I issued a privilege from Vienna permitting the Fuggers to style themselves Grafen von Kirchberg, Weissenhorn und Marstetten. 1530 is followed here as the majority reading and the NDB variant is recorded. The Diet-of-Augsburg financing negotiation itself, and the associated Cologne coronation financing of 1531, are dossier claims not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: The Diet meets in his own city, and at it Charles V and his brother press Anton and the Welsers to underwrite Ferdinand's election as King of the Romans, a crown that will be settled the following winter at Cologne with Fugger and Welser money behind it. In the same season Charles raises Anton to imperial count. He is a merchant who is now a count, in a city whose council is turning Protestant, at a Diet where the Augsburg Confession is read aloud to the emperor he is lending to. Whether the title came in 1526 or 1530 the sources still do not agree.
suggested_refs: The Diet of Augsburg, 1530
Ferdinand I's privilege of 20 June 1535 permitting the Fugger comital style of Kirchberg, Weissenhorn and Marstetten

stops.name: Augsburg, Fuggerhäuser: the coast that was granted and let go
stops.date_confidence: attested that Charles V considered and then granted the Fuggers broad concessions on the Pacific coast of South America in 1531, and that Anton let the project lapse by about 1533 (Neue Deutsche Biographie; English Wikipedia on the Fugger family). Anton never left central Europe; the stop is placed where the decision was taken, not where the grant lay. The 1532 partnership renewal making his personal command explicit is from the same source.
stops.campa: Charles V grants the house rights along the Pacific coast of South America, Peru and Chile, the kind of concession the Welsers took in Venezuela and bled for. Anton reads it and does nothing with it, and by about 1533 the grant has lapsed. He is not a man who wants a coastline four months away that has to be conquered before it pays. The money goes instead into Swabian villages he can ride to in a day. The following year the partnership is renewed on terms that put his personal command of the firm in writing.
suggested_refs: The 1531 Habsburg concession to the Fuggers on the Pacific coast of Peru and Chile, lapsed c. 1533

stops.name: Augsburg, the right to strike coin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the substance: the family receives an imperial coinage privilege as a reward tied to its finance of the crown (Neue Deutsche Biographie). No month is given.
stops.campa: The Empire grants the family the right to mint. It is payment, of a kind, for the loans that carried Ferdinand's election and Charles's wars, and it makes the house a lender that may strike the thing it lends. In February the same year the humanist Georg von Logau dedicates an edition of Ovid to Anton, who keeps a patronage circle and courted Erasmus of Rotterdam with a gold cup and an offer of a stipend to come and live in Augsburg. Erasmus kept the cup and declined the city.
suggested_refs: The imperial coinage privilege granted to the Fugger family, 1534
Georg von Logau's edition of Ovid dedicated to Anton Fugger, February 1534

stops.name: Glött, the first lordship
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1533 by the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns, 'Fuggersche Herrschaften,' which lists Glött first in Anton's acquisition series; the word Glött does not appear in the Neue Deutsche Biographie, so the dossier's citation to NDB was wrong and is corrected here. Oberndorf am Lech and Kleinkissendorf (both 1537) and Hirbishofen (1534) are itemised in the same list.
stops.campa: He buys Glött, and the buying does not stop: Hirbishofen the next year, Oberndorf am Lech and Kleinkissendorf four years after. Jakob had bought counties for the title. Anton buys villages for the jurisdiction, and jurisdiction is a different thing from a title, because a lordship comes with courts, tithes, tenants, forests, and a church whose priest the lord appoints. Money lent to an emperor can be repudiated by his son; a village has to be taken by force or not at all. Between 1533 and 1557 he acquires some seventeen of them.
suggested_refs: Schloss Glött, seat of the later Fugger-Glött line
The Fugger acquisition series of some seventeen Swabian lordships, 1533-1557

stops.name: Weißenhorn, out of a Zwinglian city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the withdrawal to Weissenhorn amid conflict with Augsburg's Protestant civic government, with a return to Augsburg around 1536 (Neue Deutsche Biographie); the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns confirms Weissenhorn as administrative centre of the Fugger lordships. The dossier's further claim of a brief detention or confinement of Anton by the Augsburg reformers is flagged by its own compiler as inconsistently reported and is not asserted here. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: Augsburg's council goes over to the Zwinglian preachers and the richest Catholic house in the city finds itself governed by men who consider its faith idolatry and its wealth theft. Anton takes his household out to Weissenhorn, the town Jakob bought in 1507, and runs the firm from there for three years, returning to Augsburg around 1536. The distance is fifty miles and the point is not the distance; a courier covers it in a day, and the ledgers come with him. The point is that a lordship has no council.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerschloss at Weissenhorn, administrative centre of the Fugger lordships

stops.name: Mickhausen, the death of Raymund
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by the Neue Deutsche Biographie ('Raymund † 1535'); the date of 3 December 1535 and the place Mickhausen are from German Wikipedia's article on Raymund Fugger. The dossier had placed this death at Augsburg, which is corrected here: Mickhausen was itself a Fugger lordship, acquired by Raymund in 1532.
stops.campa: His elder brother dies at Mickhausen, in a castle Raymund had bought for himself three years earlier: a collector, a patron of antiquities, a partner who held shares and never held command. He had spent his own money on coins, gems, and Roman marbles while his younger brother spent the firm's on emperors and villages. The two of them had been left the house together in 1525, with the command going only to the younger. What Raymund thought of that arrangement across ten years, no letter reachable in this pass records.
suggested_refs: Schloss Mickhausen, the Fugger lordship acquired by Raymund Fugger in 1532

stops.name: Donauwörth, the imperial pledge
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1536: the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns states verbatim that from 1536 the Fugger held the Reichspflege Donauwörth in pledge (Pfandbesitz). This is a pledge of an imperial office, not an outright purchase, and the Lexikon ties it to no French campaign. The dossier's association with the 1536 imperial campaign in France is not carried by that source.
stops.campa: Donauwörth is a free imperial city on the Danube and its Pflege, the imperial administrative office over it, comes into Fugger hands as a pledge against money owed. This is what a crown pays with when it has no coin: not land it owns but authority it holds. The pledge is worth exactly as much as the debt behind it, and the debt behind it is the Habsburg treasury. From 1536 Anton administers the town on the Emperor's behalf and at the Emperor's expense.
suggested_refs: The Reichspflege of Donauwörth, held in pledge by the Fugger from 1536

stops.name: Babenhausen, the castle he chose to live in
stops.date_confidence: YEAR DISPUTED three ways, not resolved. Historisches Lexikon Bayerns gives '1536/39,' a staged acquisition; German Wikipedia says Anton acquired the Burg Babenhausen in 1538; English Wikipedia says 1539. It is best written as acquired in stages between 1536 and 1539, and 1538 is used here only to order the segment. The rebuilding of the castle in 1541-1546 is confirmed verbatim by the Lexikon. The coordinate is corrected from the dossier's 48.1706, 10.4106, which is about thirteen kilometres too far east; Babenhausen (Schwaben) lies at 48° 9' N, 10° 15' E.
stops.campa: Of all the villages he buys, this is the one he moves into. He is a merchant building a seat, and a seat is a claim about the future: that there will be Fuggers here after the bank is gone. Hirbishofen, bought in 1534, is a short ride away, and the family will hold this house down to the present day. The castle comes into his hands in stages across the later 1530s, and between 1541 and 1546 he rebuilds it, generously, as a residence and not a strongpoint.
suggested_refs: Schloss Babenhausen, rebuilt by Anton Fugger 1541-1546, today housing the Fugger museum

stops.name: Augsburg, Fuggerhäuser: the last partner of his generation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the year of Hieronymus Fugger's death, which the dossier gives as 1538 and which the Neue Deutsche Biographie supports only in the general sense that Anton came to sole command. The Fugger family's formal admission to the Augsburg patriciate in the same year is a dossier claim not independently re-confirmed in this pass.
stops.campa: Hieronymus dies and there is nobody left from 1525 but Anton. Raymund three years dead at Mickhausen, Jakob thirteen, and the partnership contract that was supposed to spread the weight across three men now rests on one. Everything the house does for the next twenty-two years, every loan to Charles V, every lordship bought, every branch shut, is a decision one man makes and one man signs, with nobody left in the partnership entitled to argue. He is forty-five.
suggested_refs: The Fugger partnership after 1538, held by Anton alone among the senior partners

stops.name: Antwerp, three hundred thousand ducats
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the sum: Fuggers and Welsers raise a new 300,000-ducat loan for Charles V's wars against France and the Ottomans (Neue Deutsche Biographie), transacted between Augsburg and Antwerp. No month is given. There is no evidence Anton travelled to Antwerp; the business there ran through resident factors, named in the dossier as Veit Hörl and later Matthäus Örtel.
stops.campa: The loan is raised between Augsburg and the Antwerp bourse, where the Fugger house keeps factors and no Fugger has to stand in person: three hundred thousand ducats, jointly with the Welsers, for a war against France and a war against the Turk at the same time. On that bourse the price of money is set by strangers and moves weekly, and the Emperor's name on a bill is worth what the bourse says it is worth that morning. Veit Hörl keeps the house's books there. Later it will be Matthäus Örtel.
suggested_refs: The Fugger factory at Antwerp and its factors Veit Hörl and Matthäus Örtel

stops.name: Augsburg, five million gulden
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Neue Deutsche Biographie gives 1546 as the documented high point of the firm's capital, usually stated at about five million gulden, but the figure is a scholarly summary rather than a transcribed balance and is tagged accordingly. No month.
stops.campa: The books reach their high-water mark: about five million gulden, roughly triple what he took over in 1525. In twenty-one years Anton Fugger has more than doubled the largest private fortune in Europe. He is fifty-three. It is the last year in which the number goes up: from here on he cannot get his money back and cannot stop lending, because the debtor who owes him most is the only power that can protect what he owns. The Schmalkaldic War begins in the same summer, and he pays for that too.
suggested_refs: The Fugger balance of 1546, the documented maximum of the firm's capital

stops.name: Donauwörth, what the Emperor tells him
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION, and flagged. The dossier has Charles V secretly informing Anton at Donauwörth in 1546 that imperial resources would be turned against the Protestant Schmalkaldic League; the verification pass could not find this episode in the Neue Deutsche Biographie or any other reachable source, and it is retained as a flagged dossier lead rather than dropped. The month is not documented.
stops.campa: The story, which the reachable sources do not carry, is that the Emperor tells him here and tells him first: the army he has been raising against the Turk is going to be turned on the Lutheran princes of Germany. Anton holds the Reichspflege of this town in pledge. He is the Emperor's banker, an imperial count, and a Catholic in a country going Protestant town by town, and if the story is true he has perhaps a season to decide which of those he is. The record does not say what he said.
suggested_refs: The outbreak of the Schmalkaldic War, summer 1546
sources: Dossier lead, not confirmed against Neue Deutsche Biographie or any other reachable source in this pass

stops.name: Schwaz, the firm moves to the mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested for the withdrawal, with a route correction. The Neue Deutsche Biographie says verbatim that Anton withdrew the firm's management first to neutral Bavarian soil and only later to Schwaz in Tyrol; the dossier compressed this into a single move. The month is not documented. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: He takes the management out of Augsburg: first onto neutral Bavarian ground, then up the Inn valley to Schwaz. It is the silver mountain the house was built on and it is also the safest room in Germany that year, held by Ferdinand, out of the reach of both armies. He has been coming to this valley since 1523, when Jakob first gave him power to sign, and he is here now because the Empire below is at war. The archive travels with him. So does his wife.
suggested_refs: The Fugger company headquarters at Schwaz during the Schmalkaldic War, 1546-1547

stops.name: Augsburg, the bonds torn or burnt
stops.date_confidence: The quotation is attested: it is a memorandum by Dr. Holtzapfel in the Fugger archives, printed by Ehrenberg, who found it more credible than the folkloric versions and dated the underlying episode to after the fall of Ingolstadt in 1546. The month is Ehrenberg's chronology, not a documented date. The famous cinnamon-fire legend is separately and explicitly rejected as unevidenced by the Fugger family's own archive at fugger.de, which traces it no earlier than the end of the seventeenth century.
stops.campa: The house archive keeps a memorandum in which Anton says he has torn up or burnt certain bills of the Emperor's, so that His Majesty might see how he was minded to serve him. That is the whole of it: a line in a memorandum, written in a year when the Emperor could not pay and the creditor could not press. Out of that line grows the picture of Anton Fugger feeding Charles V's bonds into a fire of cinnamon sticks, which the family's own archive says has no contemporary evidence at all, first appears at the end of the seventeenth century, and was told of other rich merchants too. Becker painted the fire in 1866.
stops.quote: he had means in the Netherlands wherewith he would and could serve His Majesty ... but in Germany he had no other means save certain bills of His Majesty, which he had torn up or burnt in order that His Majesty might see that he was jealous to serve him with all his substance
stops.quote_source: Memorandum by Dr. Holtzapfel, Fugger Archives, quoted in Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance, trans. H. M. Lucas (London: Jonathan Cape, 1928), 118-119
suggested_refs: Carl Ludwig Friedrich Becker, 'Kaiser Karl V. bei Fugger,' 1866, Alte Nationalgalerie Berlin, exhibited Vienna 1873 and St Louis 1904
fugger.de, 'Die bekanntesten Fugger-Irrtümer,' on the debt-burning legend
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 118-119
Fürstlich und Gräflich Fuggersches Familien- und Stiftungsarchiv, fugger.de, 'Die bekanntesten Fugger-Irrtümer'

stops.name: Ulm, the Fußfall before the Emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Neue Deutsche Biographie names 'der berühmte Fußfall in Ulm' explicitly and puts Anton's return to Augsburg at the beginning of 1547. Its construction is 'nicht allein durch den berühmten Fußfall,' the kneeling being one instrument among diplomatic, financial and personal intervention, so the scene is not the whole of the mediation. The exact day is not given. The quotation is dated 26 February 1547, correcting the pool's 1546: Ehrenberg gives no year in the sentence, but his surrounding chronology runs from the Emperor's mastery of South Germany at the end of 1546 to the Wittenberg camp loan of 15 May 1547.
stops.campa: Augsburg has lost. The city that drove him out to Weissenhorn thirteen years ago now faces an emperor with an army in the field and a bill to present, and it sends its Catholic count to plead for it. At Ulm, before Charles V, Anton Fugger goes down on his knees. Civic memory kept the kneeling and made it the day Fugger saved Augsburg. He also negotiates, and pays, and works the imperial household, and the Neue Deutsche Biographie is careful to say the clemency came not by the kneeling alone.
stops.quote: the Fugger were tired of Imperial loans; they had already let themselves in so deep that they had to wait a long time before they could get their money again
stops.quote_source: Christopher Peutinger, the Welsers' representative, reporting to Augsburg, 26 February 1547, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 101
suggested_refs: The imperial headquarters at Ulm, winter 1546-1547
Ehrenberg's chronology of the Fugger loans of January-May 1547
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 101

stops.name: Schwaz, Anna dies in the mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested that Anna Fugger died at Schwaz in 1548 and was buried at Babenhausen (Neue Deutsche Biographie, which gives her dates as 1505-1548); the precise date of 25 March, her age of forty-two, and the report that death followed childbirth come from the dossier's genealogical sourcing and were not independently re-verified in this pass. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: She dies at Schwaz, where the company went for safety, in or after childbirth, forty-two years old, twenty-one years married. They bring her down out of Tyrol and bury her at Babenhausen, in the church of the village he had chosen to live in, and not in the Fugger chapel at Augsburg where his uncle lies. Twelve years later he will be laid beside her. The company he moved up here to protect had its best year on record two seasons before she died, on the same mountain his uncle first sent him to sign for a quarter of a century ago.
suggested_refs: The burial of Anna Rehlinger Fugger at Babenhausen, 1548

stops.name: Augsburg, the Fuggerei charter renewed Catholic
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly, with the source corrected. The word Fuggerei does not appear in the Neue Deutsche Biographie; the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns, 'Fuggersche Stiftungen,' gives it verbatim: on 31 July 1548 Anton Fugger renewed the foundation charter of 1521, with the Catholic condition restated and made more precise. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the last day of July he renews his uncle's foundation of 1521, the walled almshouse for the deserving poor of Augsburg, and he writes the confession into it: the tenants are to be Catholic. The city outside the gate is not. What had been a merchant's charity in a Catholic town becomes, in one clause, a Catholic enclave in a Protestant city, and it holds. It is still there, still letting rooms at a rent that is symbolic rather than commercial, now eighty-eight cents a year. Two thirds of it was bombed flat in February 1944 and rebuilt, tenants back in by September 1947.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerei, Augsburg, foundation charter of 1521 renewed 31 July 1548

stops.name: Augsburg, the Holz- und Blatternhaus
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1548, with two corrections. The Neue Deutsche Biographie does not mention the house; the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns, 'Fuggersche Stiftungen,' carries it, and attributes the two additional places created that year to a co-endowment by Veit Hörl, so Anton was not the sole founder. Hörl is separately named as a Fugger factor at Antwerp. The exact day within 1548 is set to the charter date of the other foundations of that summer.
stops.campa: He endows a house in Augsburg for the poor sick of the French pox, with a second endowment from Veit Hörl, one of his own Antwerp factors, adding two more places. The house takes its name from the wood: guaiac, shipped from the Indies, sold across Europe as the cure, and monopolised by the Fugger company. The wood does not work. Nineteen years earlier at Nuremberg, Paracelsus had said so in print and called the monopoly a fraud on the poor, and a faculty that feared the Fuggers had his syphilis tracts suppressed.
suggested_refs: The Holz- und Blatternhaus, Augsburg, 1548, co-endowed by Veit Hörl
paracelsus.journey.json, for the 1529 Nuremberg attack on the Fugger guaiac monopoly

stops.name: Waltenhausen, the hospital for fifty
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns, 'Fuggersche Stiftungen,' which gives the same charter date of 31 July 1548 and specifies places for twenty-five women and twenty-five men, correcting the dossier's implication of twenty-five in total. The word Waltenhausen does not appear in the Neue Deutsche Biographie. German Wikipedia adds that the Fuggers acquired the Waltenhausen lordship in 1541 and that the almshouse stood on the site of the Werdnau castle. The coordinate is corrected from the dossier's 48.0453, 10.2367, which lies about twenty kilometres too far south-west.
stops.campa: By the same charter of the thirty-first of July he carries out his dead cousin's bequest and founds an almshouse at Waltenhausen, on the ground of the old Werdnau castle in a lordship the family bought seven years before: twenty-five places for women and twenty-five for men, with Fugger servants, Fugger tenants, and the local poor to be taken first. Hieronymus had left the money ten years earlier. The buildings came down in 1824 and only the tithe barn is still standing.
suggested_refs: The Fugger Pfründespital at Waltenhausen, founded 31 July 1548, largely demolished 1824

stops.name: Augsburg, the will that asks to end it
stops.date_confidence: attested for the substance by the Neue Deutsche Biographie, which has Anton separating his personal interest from the Spanish business and considering dissolution while drafting a second testament in 1549-1550; the date of 22 March 1550 for the will is Ehrenberg's, who quotes it together with a codicil of 1560.
stops.campa: In his own will he writes that he wishes to bring the firm to an end and retire, because his nephews show no disposition to go on as merchants. He is fifty-seven, the richest man in Europe, the head of a house at its documented maximum four years earlier, and what he puts in the testamentary record is that he wants out. In the same months he separates his own capital from the Spanish business, which is the first move of a man preparing to be able to walk away. He does not walk away. He runs the firm for ten more years, and in those ten years the money stops coming back.
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger, will of 22 March 1550 with codicil of 1560, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 100-101
suggested_refs: Anton Fugger's second testament, 22 March 1550
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 100-101

stops.name: Villach, the asiento of the twenty-eighth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the instrument (Neue Deutsche Biographie; the dossier cites Pölnitz's dedicated article 'Der Asiento Karls V. vom 28.5.1552,' which was not fetched in this pass). No evidence was found that Anton was personally at Villach; the asiento may have been negotiated by agents while he was at Augsburg or Schwaz. The quotation is from letters of 1553-1554 and is placed here for its subject, not its date.
stops.campa: Charles V is running from Maurice of Saxony through the Alps with an army behind him and no money in front of him, and at Villach the Fugger house signs the asiento that keeps him solvent. It is the same transaction as 1529 and 1543 and 1547, made under worse terms because the need is worse. The Emperor survives the Princes' Revolt. The debt does not get smaller. On the state of the Empire itself, Anton writes to his factor in Antwerp the year after.
stops.quote: It is not good that His Imperial Majesty cometh not (to the Empire) and that the Diet falls into the water and Germany becometh a bears' den where each man doeth what he listeth
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger, letters to Matthäus Oertel, 1553-1554, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 110
suggested_refs: The Asiento of Villach, 28 May 1552
Götz von Pölnitz, 'Der Asiento Karls V. vom 28.5.1552'
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 110

stops.name: Constantinople, the old factor sent east
stops.date_confidence: attested with a date correction: the Neue Deutsche Biographie says verbatim that Anton sent the Altfaktor, the senior or former factor, Hans Dernschwam to Turkey in 1553/55, so the mission is a two-year range and not a single year. NDB does not mention Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq; the connection to Busbecq's Habsburg embassy is real in the wider literature but is not carried by the cited source and is not asserted here. Anton did not travel; the pin marks where his man went.
stops.campa: He sends Hans Dernschwam, an old factor of the house who had run the Hungarian mines, east into Ottoman territory for two years. What comes back is not a contract. It is a description: of Constantinople, of Anatolia, of Greek inscriptions copied off stones, of a country the merchants of Augsburg had financed three wars against and never looked at. Anton Fugger himself never leaves central Europe. He is sixty, with a coast in Peru he did not take and a factor in Anatolia he did send. Dernschwam is away until 1555 and writes the whole way.
suggested_refs: Hans Dernschwam's Tagebuch of his journey to Constantinople and Asia Minor, 1553-1555

stops.name: Augsburg, the letters to Antwerp
stops.date_confidence: attested as a quotation: Ehrenberg dates the letter to Matthäus Oertel to late 1553. No day is given, defaulted to 01-01. Ehrenberg's spelling of the factor's name is Oertel; the Neue Deutsche Biographie writes Örtel.
stops.campa: The letters to his Antwerp factor across these years are a running account of not being paid. No resolution as to the debts will come from the court; the court is busy; the affairs are tedious and hazardous. He writes it plainly and he goes on lending, because the alternative to lending to Charles V is admitting that what has already been lent will never come back. The largest creditor in Europe is writing to a clerk in Flanders about a debtor who does not answer his post. Ehrenberg dates the letter to late 1553.
stops.quote: no Resolution as to our debts will come from the Court. Verily in these heavy times they have much else to do, but it is yet hazardous and these affairs are tedious
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger to Matthäus Oertel, late 1553, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 109-110
suggested_refs: The Anton Fugger-Oertel correspondence in the Fugger archives, as printed by Ehrenberg
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 109-110

stops.name: Almadén, the mercury given up
stops.date_confidence: attested for the withdrawal from Spain across 1542-1553, when Anton renounced the Maestrazgo lease and gave up the Guadalcanal silver mines (English Wikipedia, 'Fugger'); the year 1553 is the close of that range. Anton never visited Spain; the mercury and cinnabar of Almadén were a contractual security managed through agents. The convict-labour regime at Almadén began in 1566, six years after his death, and is not attributable to him. Pin inherited byte-identical from jakob_fugger_the_rich.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Spanish business is always the same trade: lend the crown money, take the revenues of the military orders and the mercury of Almadén as security. Mercury amalgamates American silver, so whoever holds Almadén holds one end of the world's money supply. Anton lets it go, along with the Guadalcanal silver mines and the Maestrazgo lease, over a decade of steady withdrawal that begins in 1542 and is finished by 1553. He never sees Spain; the mines are a security clause worked by agents. He gives his factor a reason, and the reason is an interest rate.
stops.quote: for if I lay the money on finance (short term loans) it bears 12 per cent
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger, order regarding a debt renewal, 1553, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 109
suggested_refs: The Almadén cinnabar and mercury mines held as security against Spanish asientos
The Maestrazgo revenues of the Spanish military orders
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 109

stops.name: Augsburg, an Augsburg debt and men's mockery
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ehrenberg dates both phrases to February 1554, in an order to Oertel to raise money against a debt owed at Augsburg, printing 'for my credit stands thereon' and immediately after it the sentence quoted here. The day is not given.
stops.campa: He orders his factor to raise money for a debt falling due at Augsburg, and gives two reasons in the space of a line: his credit stands on it, and he thinks as much about being laughed at as about the money. This from a man whose grandfather came into this city as a weaver from Graben and whose own council has told him twice in twenty years what it thinks of his house and his faith. The debt is small and he can pay it out of a pocket. What he cannot do, in the city where the family made itself, is be seen not paying it.
stops.quote: I think as much on men's mockery as on the money itself
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger to Matthäus Oertel, February 1554, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 110
suggested_refs: Ehrenberg's transcription of Anton Fugger's February 1554 order to Oertel
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 110

stops.name: Augsburg, the Christmas payment prolonged till Easter
stops.date_confidence: attested and page-corrected: the quotation appears at Ehrenberg (1928), 280, not at 276-277 as the pool had it. The 1557 date and Ehrenberg's editorial comment are correct as given. No day.
stops.campa: Antwerp postpones its Christmas settlement to Easter and Anton, who has spent thirty years on that bourse through factors, writes that since one can do no otherwise and there is no harm in it, he must let it be. In the same year Spain declares the first of its state bankruptcies, and the firm never recovers the ground it loses by it. Ehrenberg reads the line as evidence of how little the greatest financier of his time understood, in his old age, the relation between the government of the Netherlands and the city of Antwerp.
stops.quote: I have learnt that the Christmas payment is to be prolonged till Easter, and that the city of Antwerp will thus help itself out; since one can do no otherwise and there is no harm in it, I must let it be
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger to his Antwerp agent, 1557, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 280
suggested_refs: The Antwerp credit crisis and the Spanish state bankruptcy of 1557
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 280

stops.name: Augsburg, Örtel dismissed and the silver seized
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the substance by the Neue Deutsche Biographie: the Antwerp factor Matthäus Örtel made unauthorised deals with Philip II, Spanish authorities seized Fugger silver transports, and Anton dismissed him and cut the Spanish investment. No month is documented. The loss from Spain's 1557 bankruptcy is independently confirmed by fugger.de as the start of the firm's decline.
stops.campa: His own man in Antwerp has been dealing with Philip II without authority, and in Spain the crown's officers seize Fugger silver in transit. Anton had written to him many times that he was not to trust the court, and this is the man who kept the house's books at Antwerp through the loans of 1543 and the bankruptcy year of 1557. He is sixty-four and chronically ill, running a bank whose largest positions are now losses. He dismisses Örtel, pulls what is left out of Spain, and winds down the Weissenhorn textile works.
stops.quote: The devil thank you for this agency
stops.quote_source: Anton Fugger to Matthäus Oertel, 1557, quoted in Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 115
suggested_refs: The seizure of Fugger silver transports by Spanish authorities, 1557
sources: Richard Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance (1928), 115

stops.name: Augsburg, the third will and the Schneidhaus
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION RESOLVED, and the resolution recorded. The Fugger Archive catalogue at paperinmotion.org dates the will to 1 November 1560, after Anton's death on 14 September; the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns independently dates his Schneidhaus endowment to 26 July 1560, before the death, and specifies its purpose as the surgical removal of bladder stones. The November date is therefore read as probate or registration rather than composition. The 57 legacies, the 10,900 gulden total and the 1,000 gulden for alms agree across both sources; the recipient-by-recipient amounts in the catalogue record diverge in detail from the dossier's flat summary.
stops.campa: Seven weeks before he dies he adds the last provisions: fifty-seven legacies, ten thousand nine hundred gulden, another thousand for alms, and a surgical foundation, the Schneidhaus, to pay for cutting bladder stones out of poor men. The man who lent the Emperor five million gulden is settling sums of two hundred. Two lawyers get twelve hundred each, four clerks three hundred each, the Spanish representative four hundred, his chief accountant Matthäus Schwarz two hundred, then the household servants, by name.
suggested_refs: Anton Fugger's third testament, 26 July 1560, and the Schneidhaus foundation for bladder-stone surgery
The Fugger Archive catalogue record of the will, paperinmotion.org
sources: paperinmotion.org, 'Last will and testament of Anton Fugger'

stops.name: Augsburg, death in his own house
stops.date_confidence: attested and independently confirmed by three fetched sources: the Neue Deutsche Biographie ('Nach langem Leiden verschied F. am 14.9.1560 zu Augsburg'), English Wikipedia and German Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He dies at Augsburg after a long illness, sixty-seven years old, thirty-five years at the head of the house. He had asked in writing ten years earlier to be allowed to stop. He left no book, no memoir, nothing an editor could later publish as a work: the only thing he wrote that survives as his own is a Titelbuch, a chancery manual for addressing princes and prelates correctly, which has never been printed. What is his and still standing is the almshouse, the archive, and the villages. In 1997 Augsburg named a new bridge over the Lech after him.
suggested_refs: The Anton-Fugger-Brücke over the Lech at Augsburg, named 1997
Götz von Pölnitz, 'Das Titelbuch des Anton Fugger,' Archivalische Zeitschrift 50/51 (1955), the only study of the manuscript, which has never been printed as an edition
sources: Götz von Pölnitz, 'Das Titelbuch des Anton Fugger' (1955), cited via the dossier bibliography; the article itself was not fetched

stops.name: Babenhausen, St Andreas: buried away from Augsburg
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial at Babenhausen (Neue Deutsche Biographie, 'Beigesetzt in Babenhausen'); German Wikipedia's article on St Andreas states that the parish church was designated Hauptkirche and Grablege of the family after Anton acquired the lordship. The exact date of the funeral is not documented and 20 September is an ordering device. The interpretation that the move from Augsburg followed St Anna's passing into Protestant hands is the dossier's framing, not a sourced statement. The coordinate is corrected as at the earlier Babenhausen stop.
stops.campa: They do not take him to St Anna in Augsburg, where Jakob lies under the chapel the family built, because that church is Protestant now and the family's dead have been moving out of the city for twelve years. They bury him at Babenhausen instead, in the parish church of the village he bought and rebuilt and lived in, beside Anna. The chapel at St Anna is still standing in Augsburg, empty of him, in a Protestant parish church. The castle at Babenhausen holds the Fugger museum today.
suggested_refs: St Andreas, Babenhausen, Hauptkirche and Grablege of the Fugger family
The Fuggerkapelle at St Anna, Augsburg, built by Jakob Fugger and now in a Protestant church
